question: Which statistical-physics mechanisms connect low-temperature glasses, rigidity transitions in continuous constraint problems, and the dynamics of high-dimensional inference and learning algorithms?

key_findings.claim: The KHGPS soft-spin model separates two zero-temperature routes to replica-symmetry breaking that have different low-frequency excitations.
key_findings.evidence: At small external field, the replicon bound is saturated, spin-glass susceptibility diverges, and the Hessian density gives delocalized D(omega) proportional to omega^2 modes. At larger field, local effective potentials first develop double wells while the replicon is still positive; the transition instead produces localized D(omega) proportional to omega^4 modes and a pseudogap in nearly degenerate two-level systems. The latter is proposed as a more plausible finite-dimensional mechanism because it need not show a divergent linear susceptibility.

1.3.5 Two Mechanisms for the Spin Glass Transition

key_findings.claim: Across sphere packings, perceptrons, multilayer random classifiers, nonspherical particles, and tissue-inspired models, constraint geometry and isostaticity organize distinct rigidity universality classes.
key_findings.evidence: The review argues that nonconvex isostatic problems with replica-symmetry breaking reproduce the sphere-jamming scaling solution and power-law force/gap statistics, including through dimensional reduction in multidimensional constraints. Extra degrees of freedom can yield hypostatic jamming with different nonsingular scaling. Marginal stability alone is judged insufficient; self-similarity and stochastic stability over accessible configurations are proposed as the ingredients that select exponents.

key_findings.claim: Dynamical mean-field theory exposes an algorithmic hierarchy in stylized high-dimensional inference: glassiness can trap generic sampling or gradient dynamics before approximate message passing fails.
key_findings.evidence: For sparse spiked matrix and mixed spiked matrix-tensor models, metastable uninformative states create an information-computation gap. AMP follows a state-evolution/free-energy fixed point, whereas exact high-dimensional DMFT shows Langevin and gradient descent relaxation times diverging at lower noise than the AMP recovery boundary. Conversely, exponentially many spurious minima alone do not determine failure: gradient descent can recover beyond the landscape's topology-trivialization line.

key_findings.claim: Mini-batch stochasticity can improve signal recovery over full-batch gradient descent in controlled nonconvex problems, but the demonstrated regime remains far from modern overparameterized networks.
key_findings.evidence: DMFT characterizes SGD and persistent-SGD as state-dependent driven dynamics rather than equilibrium thermal noise. Phase-retrieval experiments suggest better recovery but suffer large finite-size and long-time integration limits; a Gaussian matrix measurement model permits longer DMFT integration and shows a lower sample-complexity recovery threshold for small-batch SGD than GD. The author stresses that these results are mainly underparameterized inference settings and calls for overparameterized network models linking landscape geometry to generalization.

method.core_idea: Use solvable disordered mean-field models to isolate universal mechanisms—replica-symmetry breaking, marginal/isostatic stability, glassy metastability, and driven noise—then compare their implications across physical systems and learning algorithms.
method.mechanism: The HDR synthesis combines replica/cavity analyses of equilibrium order parameters, Hessian spectra and pseudogaps; continuous constraint-satisfaction mappings and jamming scaling; approximate-message-passing state evolution; Kac-Rice landscape counts; and dynamical mean-field equations for Langevin, GD, SGD, and persistent-SGD. It reviews the author's prior papers, highlights selected new conceptual arguments, and routes detailed derivations to the originals.
assumptions: Mean-field or infinite-dimensional limits reveal mechanisms that may persist, with renormalization, in finite dimensions.
Quenched disorder, self-averaging, and replica/cavity saddle points adequately represent the selected systems.
Simple spiked, perceptron, phase-retrieval, and Gaussian measurement models are informative proxies for real inference and neural learning.
Long-time algorithm behavior can be inferred from numerically integrated DMFT and finite-size simulations where explicit solutions are unavailable.
Universality is controlled by constraint geometry, isostaticity, and accessible-state stability rather than microscopic details alone.

techniques.role: Characterizes glass phases, stability bounds, pseudogaps, and effective local potentials.
Distinguishes localized quartic from delocalized quadratic soft-mode regimes.
Connects packings, tissues, perceptrons, and neural fitting through SAT/UNSAT rigidity.
Relates contact counting, marginality, pseudogaps, and universal critical exponents.
Reduces high-dimensional stochastic/gradient dynamics to self-consistent correlation and response equations.
Separates information-theoretic, AMP, Langevin, GD, and SGD recovery thresholds.

evaluations.setting: Zero-temperature KHGPS model over interaction strength and external field
evaluations.metric: Replica stability, Hessian spectral gap/exponent, localization, and spin-glass susceptibility
evaluations.result: Two transition mechanisms yield respectively delocalized omega-squared and localized omega-fourth-power low-frequency spectra.
evaluations.baseline: SK/KH-like mean-field spin glasses with only the linear-instability route

evaluations.setting: Analytic and numerical continuous-CSP models near SAT/UNSAT or rigidity transitions
evaluations.metric: Contact number, force/gap distributions, replica symmetry, and scaling exponents
evaluations.result: Isostatic nonconvex models collapse to the sphere-jamming class, while additional degrees of freedom can create a hypostatic class.
evaluations.baseline: Infinite-dimensional spheres and the one-field nonconvex perceptron

evaluations.setting: Spiked matrix-tensor inference in the high-dimensional limit
evaluations.metric: Noise level at signal recovery and divergence of relaxation time
evaluations.result: Langevin and GD fail in glassy regions where AMP still recovers; GD success extends into a landscape with exponentially many spurious minima.
evaluations.baseline: Approximate Message Passing and information-theoretic transition lines

evaluations.setting: Phase retrieval and nonlinear Gaussian signal recovery
evaluations.metric: Sample-complexity recovery threshold and relaxation-time extrapolation
evaluations.result: Small-batch SGD/persistent-SGD empirically and, in the simpler model, through DMFT reaches signal recovery below the GD threshold.
evaluations.baseline: Full-batch gradient descent and Langevin dynamics

limitations: This is an HDR synthesis of the author's research program, not a systematic review; selection and interpretation are intentionally personal.
Most technical derivations are omitted and delegated to the underlying papers, so several claims cannot be independently reconstructed from this manuscript alone.
Replica calculations and mean-field/infinite-dimensional models do not by themselves establish which critical behavior survives in two or three dimensions.
The learning results use stylized, often underparameterized teacher-student inference problems rather than deep, overparameterized networks or natural data.
Numerical integration of DMFT is time-limited, and recovery thresholds in phase retrieval have substantial finite-size/long-time uncertainty.
AMP's advantage relies on matched probabilistic structure; the manuscript acknowledges its limited robustness to unknown or mismatched data-generating processes.
No unified experiment tests the proposed conceptual bridge from physical marginality to neural-network generalization.
failure_modes: A mean-field TLS transition is rounded or absent in finite dimension despite the proposed mechanism.
Replica analytic continuation or assumed symmetry-breaking ansatz selects the wrong physical saddle.
Isostaticity holds while different constraint correlations or dynamics change the critical exponents.
An apparent algorithmic threshold is a finite-time crossover rather than a true high-dimensional transition.
AMP is brittle under distribution mismatch, while a nominally inferior generic optimizer succeeds on real data.
SGD noise helps escape the selected toy landscape but harms optimization or generalization in an overparameterized network.
Landscape counts fail to predict which atypical minima are dynamically accessible from realistic initialization.
reusable_insights: Separate linear soft modes from nonlinear two-level rearrangements when diagnosing marginal systems.
Classify constraint problems by isostatic versus hypostatic organization before comparing critical exponents.
Benchmark optimizers against information-theoretic and algorithm-specific phase boundaries, not training loss alone.
Track correlation, response, and relaxation time jointly when a driven optimizer has state-dependent noise.
Do not infer optimization failure merely from exponentially many stationary points; characterize dynamically selected states.
Use solvable models as mechanism probes, then explicitly test which conclusions survive dimensionality, mismatch, and overparameterization.
open_questions: What finite-dimensional field theory captures pseudogapped nonlinear excitations and their spatial size?
Can self-similarity or stochastic stability of accessible configurations determine jamming exponents without replicas?
Which properties of isostatic criticality remain super-universal under correlated constraints and finite-dimensional fluctuations?
Can DMFT be extended to realistic overparameterized multilayer networks at useful time horizons?
How do SGD's driven noise, loss geometry, flatness, and test generalization causally interact?
Can robust message-passing methods retain their threshold advantage under model mismatch?
Which observables predict algorithmic recovery when early-time dynamics select atypical regions of the landscape?

competitive_landscape.title: Low-frequency vibrational spectrum of mean-field disordered systems
competitive_landscape.difference: Bouchbinder et al. supply the exact KHGPS phase diagram and the omega-squared/delocalized versus omega-fourth-power/localized spectral result. The reviewed HDR embeds that result in a broader claim about spin-glass transitions, nonlinear excitations, and finite dimensions.

competitive_landscape.title: Field theory for zero temperature soft anharmonic spin glasses in a field
competitive_landscape.difference: Urbani constructs the finite-dimensional loop expansion and finds a positive replicon mass but singular cubic couplings in the nonlinear-transition regime. It is a concrete extension of, but not yet a completed answer to, the HDR's finite-dimensional question.

competitive_landscape.title: Jamming in multilayer supervised learning models
competitive_landscape.difference: Franz, Hwang, and Urbani show analytically and numerically that multidimensional multilayer constraints recover sphere-jamming scaling when they are isostatic. The HDR generalizes this into a classification program spanning equality/inequality and isostatic/hypostatic systems.

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent outperforms Gradient Descent in recovering a high-dimensional signal in a glassy energy landscape
competitive_landscape.difference: Kamali and Urbani provide the DMFT and relaxation-time evidence behind the small-batch SGD recovery advantage. The HDR is more cautious about generalization, emphasizing that the model is a controlled inference proxy rather than a modern neural-network result.

novelty_assessment: The manuscript's value is a coherent, unusually candid synthesis across three mature lines of the author's work: nonlinear versus linear glass instabilities, constraint-geometry universality, and DMFT benchmarks of learning dynamics. Most headline results were published earlier and the author explicitly omits many derivations; novelty lies in the cross-domain organizing claims, selected scaling interpretation, and research agenda. Those bridges are generative but remain hypotheses until tested outside mean-field and stylized inference models.
reviewer_notes: Read the full 117-page HDR, including scope/originality caveats, all chapter conclusions and perspectives, the KHGPS phase mechanism, CCSP scaling synthesis, AMP/GD/Langevin phase diagrams, and SGD/persistent-SGD discussion. This record treats it as a research-program synthesis rather than attributing every reviewed result as new in 2024. Four primary arXiv component papers were checked on 2026-08-23.
